content: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease primarily affecting the joints, characterized by inflammation, pain, swelling, stiffness, and potential joint damage. It involves the immune system mistakenly attacking the synovium (joint lining), triggering inflammation that can lead to cartilage and bone erosion. This systemic condition may also affect organs beyond joints, such as eyes and lungs. RA is distinct from osteoarthritis, which is caused by wear and tear rather than immune-mediated inflammation. Major synonyms and abbreviations include RA and chronic inflammatory arthritis. The exact cause remains unknown but involves genetic, environmental, and hormonal factors. Early diagnosis and treatment are critical to prevent irreversible joint damage and disability. Diagnostic evaluation typically includes clinical examination, laboratory tests assessing markers such as rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies, and imaging studies like X-rays and ultrasound. Treatment strategies prioritize controlling inflammation and maintaining function through medications including disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), biologics, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and glucocorticoids. Lifestyle adjustments like physical therapy, regular exercise, and diet modifications can complement medical therapy. Safety considerations include potential medication side effects, infection risks, and importance of patient monitoring. Limitations in current evidence exist regarding exact disease mechanisms and long-term outcomes of novel therapies, making ongoing research essential. This module covers comprehensive aspects of RA, providing understandable and practical knowledge for consumers and healthcare providers alike, supporting informed decisions and improved management.

content: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disorder in which the body's immune system attacks its own tissues, mainly targeting the synovium—the lining of the joints. This results in inflammation manifesting as pain, swelling, warmth, and stiffness in affected joints. Unlike osteoarthritis, which stems from joint wear and tear, RA is a systemic condition meaning it can affect organs such as lungs, heart, and eyes. It typically affects small joints of the hands and feet symmetrically, but larger joints can also be involved. RA is chronic and can cause joint damage and disability if left untreated.

content: The exact cause of RA is unknown, but it involves a complex interplay of genetic and environmental factors triggering an abnormal immune response. The immune system produces autoantibodies, such as rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies, that attack joint tissues, leading to persistent inflammation. This inflammation causes pannus formation, which invades cartilage and bone, causing damage. Environmental factors like smoking and infections may increase risk. Hormonal influences are suspected since RA is more common in women.

content: Several risk factors increase the likelihood of developing RA. Genetic predisposition plays a role, especially certain human leukocyte antigen (HLA) gene variants like HLA-DRB1. Women are two to three times more likely to develop RA than men, possibly due to hormonal influences. Smoking is a major modifiable risk factor. Age is relevant; RA most commonly begins between ages 30-60. Family history and certain environmental exposures are also linked to increased risk.

content: Symptoms of RA commonly include joint pain, swelling, stiffness especially in the morning lasting more than 30 minutes, and symmetrical involvement of joints. Fatigue, low-grade fever, and generalized weakness can occur. As the disease progresses, joint deformities and loss of function may develop. Systemic symptoms include dry eyes, nodules under the skin (rheumatoid nodules), and inflammation in other organs like lungs or heart.

content: Diagnosis relies on a combination of clinical evaluation, laboratory testing, and imaging. Blood tests typically measure rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-CCP antibodies, both markers of autoimmunity. Elevated inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) support active inflammation. Imaging with X-rays, ultrasound, or MRI can reveal joint space narrowing, erosions, and synovitis. Criteria established by the American College of Rheumatology and European League Against Rheumatism inform diagnosis.

content: RA treatment aims to reduce inflammation, relieve symptoms, prevent joint damage, and improve quality of life. Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) like methotrexate are first-line therapy to slow disease progression. Biologic agents targeting immune molecules (e.g., TNF inhibitors) are used if DMARDs are insufficient. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and corticosteroids help control symptoms but do not prevent damage. Physical therapy and occupational therapy support joint function and mobility.

content: Lifestyle changes complement medical treatments to manage RA effectively. Regular low-impact exercises like swimming and walking maintain joint flexibility and muscle strength without excessive strain. Balanced nutrition supports overall health; omega-3 fatty acids may reduce inflammation. Smoking cessation is crucial to reduce disease severity and improve medication response. Adequate rest prevents fatigue, while joint protection techniques preserve function.

content: Beyond joints, RA can cause complications including cardiovascular disease, lung inflammation (interstitial lung disease), osteoporosis, and increased infection risk due to both disease and medications. Rheumatoid nodules can develop in skin and organs. Chronic inflammation contributes to accelerated atherosclerosis. Early recognition and management of comorbidities are essential for improved outcomes.

content: Treatments for RA, particularly immunosuppressive medications like DMARDs and biologics, carry risks such as increased susceptibility to infections and potential liver or kidney toxicity. Regular monitoring through blood tests and clinical evaluation is needed. Vaccinations should be updated prior to starting immunosuppressive therapy. Patients must communicate any infections or side effects promptly to healthcare providers.

content: A frequent misconception is that RA is simply wear-and-tear arthritis; however, RA results from autoimmune inflammation requiring different treatment. Some believe RA only affects joints, but it can involve organs systemically. Another myth is that RA always causes visible joint deformities early on; symptoms and progression vary. Understanding these realities helps patients seek appropriate care and avoid stigma.

chunk_title: Prognosis and Importance of Early Treatment
content: While RA is a chronic disease without a cure, early and aggressive treatment can induce remission or low disease activity, preventing joint damage and disability. Delayed treatment is linked to worse outcomes. Continuous monitoring and treatment adjustments are necessary to manage flares and maintain function. Patient education and engagement improve adherence and quality of life.
